speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall occupy but a few moments of the time of the house, and I do so from a sense of duty which I believe I cannot evade. I desire to refer to certain important questions which have been raised in the course of this debate. While I have been unable to attend the opening sessions of the house, I have followed with the deepest interest the proceedings and the various discussions which have taken place. Never was I so proud of my membership in this house as when I read the speeches which were made in this chamber in approval of the resolution presented on the treaty to outlaw war. The debate was on a high plane throughout and would have done credit to any legislative body in the world. The true international spirit was apparent and manifested itself in all the views which were then expressed, and from all sides came the unqualified offer of the most intense cooperation for the furtherance of all moves which might lead to the establishment of permanent peace.
The world has moved forward; a new psychology of peace is gradually replacing the war psychology of the past, and it is no longer a sign of inferiority, a sort of inglorious stigma, to preach and advocate peace. Indeed, of all the beneficent effects of the League of Nations none is perhaps more commendable than the creation of a new international conscience whose feelings, whether or not they are officially expressed, are recognized and respected everywhere even by material strength and military power. This is the new international conscience which has given birth to the Kellogg pact and which has induced so many nations to accept compulsory arbitration of conflicts between states in order to replace violence and force by the rules of law and international justice. Nobody can fail to realize the supreme importance of a public act by which all the nations joined

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe
together to declare that peace is the only goal to be reached and that war should be outlawed and denounced.
But the value of this agreement will depend largely upon the subsequent measures, upon the steps which will be taken everywhere by all nations for the purpose of reaching what they all declare to be their goal. Peace will be secured if nations can eliminate as far as possible the usual causes of conflicts, the ordinary sources of difficulties. The League of Nations has been during the last few years and is now investigating what those sources of difficulties and causes of conflict are.
I am going to refer now to what has been declared to be the main source of difficulties between nations and this brings me directly to the subject under debate. On the 26th September, 1925, the assembly of the League of Nations adopted this resolution:
The assembly, firmly resolved to seek all possible means of establishing peace throughout the world; convinced that economic peace will largely contribute to security among the nations; persuaded of the necessity of investigating the economic difficulties which stand in the way of the revival of general prosperity, and of ascertaining the best means of overcoming these difficulties and of preventing disputes; invites the council to consider at the earliest possible moment the expediency of constituting on a wide basis a preparatory committee which, with the assistance of technical organizations of the league and the International Labour Office, will prepare the work of an international economic conference.
The convening of this conference under the auspices of the League of Nations shall be a matter for subsequent decision by the council.
The council took action on that recommendation and organized the preparatory committee composed of leading men of many nations. This preparatory committee started to work and organized an economic conference which sat in Geneva on the 4th May, 1927, and whose session extended until the 23rd May, 1927. The members of this conference were appointed by the various governments. Other members were nominated by the council or by certain international organizations invited by the council and experts accompanied members or were invited by the president of the conference. It consisted of 194 delegates and 226 experts representing 50 states, some of which were not and are not now members of the league. The president of the conference was M. Theunis, a former premier of Belgium. One of the vice-presidents was Mr. Henry M. Robinson, an American representative. Oanada was represented at that conference by the following;

The conference divided itself into committees, the three main committees being one on agriculture, one on commerce, and one on industry. I have the official report of the conference here which, after discussion, was presented and adopted by the conference. I am sorry that time will not permit me to read some of the very important considerations in that report as to commercial policies. I shall confine myself to reading the conclusion :
In view of the fact that harmful effects upon production and trade result from the high and constantly changing tariffs which are applied in many countries;
The Budget-Mr. Lapointe

And since substantial improvement in the economic conditions can be obtained by increased facilities for international trade and commerce;
And in view of the fact that tariffs, though within the sovereign jurisdiction of the separate states, are not a matter of purely domestic interest but greatly influence the trade of the world;
And in view of the fact that some of the causes which have resulted in the increase of tariffs and in other trade barriers since the war have largely disappeared and others are diminishing;
The conference declares that the time has come to put an end to the increase in tariffs and to move in the opposite direction.
The conference recommends:
(1)	That nations should take steps forthwith to remove or diminish those tariff barriers that gravely hamper trade, starting with those which have been imposed to counteract the effects of disturbances arising out of the war.
_ Moreover, in order to ensure that this action is continuously pursued, the conference recommends:
(2)	That states should proceed to the conclusion of commercial treaties on lines and under conditions calculated to ensure the attainment of the aims mentioned herein;
(3)	That, in future, the practice of putting into force, in advance of negotiations, excessive duties established for the purpose of bargaining, whether by means of tarifs de combat or by means of general tariffs, should be abandoned;
(4)	That the Council of the League of Nations should be requested to instruct its economic organization to examine on the basis of the principles enunciated by the present conference, the possibility of further action by the respective states with a view to promoting the equitable treatment of commerce by eliminating or reducing the obstructions which excessive Customs tariffs offer to international trade.
In this enquiry, the economic organization should consult with representatives of the various governments, including non-members of the league, and also so far as necessary with the competent bodies representing commerce, industry, agriculture and labour.
The object of the enquiry should be to encourage the extension of international trade on an equitable basis, while at the same time paying due regard to the just interests of producers and workers in obtaining a fair remuneration and of consumers in increasing their purchasing power.	.
I will quote one sentence from the general resolutions in the final report with respect to agriculture:
It is desirable that all hindrances to the free circulation of and trade in agricultural products should be removed, in so far as their removal does not endanger the vital interests of rne different countries and their workers.
In those states in which customs protection is maintained, it should be reduced, both for industry^ and agriculture, to the lowest possible point indispensable to production; care should be taken to assist in the maintenance .of an equitable balance between industry and agriculture and not to stifle one to the advantage of the other.

The final resolution concerning economic tendencies affecting the peace of the world reads:
The conference:
Recognizing that the maintenance of world peace depends largely upon the principles on which the economic policies of nations are framed and executed:
Recommends that the governments and peoples of the countries here represented should together give continuous attention to this aspect of the economic problem, and looks forward to the establishment of recognized principles designed to eliminate those economic difficulties which cause friction and misunsder-standing in a w-orld which has everything to gain from peaceful and harmonious progress.
The conference recognizes that the reception and successful application of the principles stated in the resolutions of the conference depend, not only upon the good-will of governments and administrations, but upon an informed and supporting public opinion throughout the world, and for this purpose would welcome, in the economic as in other fields, the development of closer international cooperation by scientific and educational institutions, as well as the help of the press and other agencies of importance for the information and enlightenment of the public.
These recommendations were unanimously adopted by the conference except for the union of Soviet republics of Russia and Turkey. These recommendations were afterwards approved by the council of the league, which recommended that as far as possible they should be carried out by the various nations Which had taken part in the conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is one of the regrets
of my life that what I say is always unpleasant to my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Air. Cahan), although it is so far from my wish and my purpose. We have put those principles into practice in spite of the protests and notwithstanding the objections of many who preach in this country the very doctrine which they denounce as selfish hostility when it is practised by other countries. Rut. sir, the conditions in Canada to-day show that the economic conference was right when it formulated those principles as being sound economically for the progress of the various nations of the world. I do not think we have increased any item of our tariff since 1921, and we have reduced many. We may say, with a certain amount of pride too, that those who year in and year out were predicting blue ruin and bankruptcy and disaster, are compelled to-day to thank or to blame Providence for the prosperity now en-jojmd by Canada, for the buoyant conditions in transportation, in banking, in industry, for the large and expanding trade of this country -all figures speak with such a loud voice that the whispers of death have been silenced, I hope forever.
But, Mr. Speaker, there are other statements in the report I have read which to-day are also proved to be true in the clearest possible manner. What better evidence could we have of the danger of high protective tariffs, of their inherent menace to the peace of the world and to good international relations, than the words which have been uttered in this house at the mere suggestion of a possible increase of customs duties by the country to the south of us? Appeals have even been made to " red-blooded Canadians " for retaliatory action, suggestions have been made that parliament ought to adjourn or to prolong its sittings to take counteraction. It has even been suggested that the governor in council should be empowered to increase our tariff schedules should the necessity arise. Sir, the tariff policies of other countries are their own business-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and certainly I will not venture to express any opinion thereon, except the hope that the apostles of high and higher tariff duties will not be more successful in other countries than they have been in this in carrying out a policy which

was denounced so energetically and so unanimously by the representatives of all the countries sitting in conference in 1927.
But what if they succeed? Well, I believe that the Canadian people will not lose their heads. I am confident they will continue to trust the safe and sound judgment and the good, logical common-sense mind of my Scotch friend, the Minister of Finance, to deal with the situation. Those issues cannot be fought with heat and prejudice. If one market is closed to us, it is evident that we will have to find other markets; and if one market is made more difficult for our goods to enter, we will have to find other markets which are accessible. If it is necessary to modify certain tariff schedules for the purpose of developing a larger trade with nations which are desirous of trading with us, this may be done, but only in the Canadian interest and not at all as a result of a policy of retaliation or tariff war. In doing this, I repeat, Canadian interests, and Canadian interest alone, must be considered. Talk of red blood! Is it a manifestation of red blood to shape our tariff policies on the policies of foreign countries by imitation or in any other manner? Did it show a lack of dignity, was it a shameless action on the part of Britain to maintain her policies though her neighbours in the adjoining countries had protectionist tariffs, such as France, Germany and other nations? I know of no prouder words than those uttered by Sir Robert Peel in 1846 when, speaking to a world encircled by protectionist tariffs, he said:	No matter what foreign countries do
in the matter of removing their tariffs or not, Britain will act in her own way and in her own interests. And that Sir Robert Peel and other Britons were men of red blood no one could ever deny. The same words, or practically the same words were uttered by Mr. Asquith in 1903 when he replied to the argument for retaliation as set forth by Mr. Joseph Chamberlain. .
Our neighbours will shape their policies in Washington and we will shape our policies in Ottawa in the interests of the Canadian people and in accordance with their views. Whatever may be my admiration for other countries, it does not go ito the point of necessarily copying their methods and their policies and of looking at some social and political problems in the same way as they look at them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not even if expressed by an economic conference?

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will my ihon. friend allow me to proceed?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Though I do not resent anything coming from him, my time is limited. As I was saying, whatever may be my admiration for other countries I still prefer the Canadian vision, the Canadian mentality, the Canadian outlook, and I deem it very important to preserve our own national characteristics and maintain our own way of dealing with public questions. May I remark furthermore that I have never noticed a keen desire on the part of my protectionist friends to imitate even the United States when that country happened to lean towards freer trade.
I know of some items which are being admitted free into that country and which are paying a duty in Canada; and they are of some importance. But, as I say, I have never yet witnessed any demand on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite for reciprocity so far as these items are concerned. I will not refer either to the reciprocity agreement of 1911 except perhaps to observe that only the other-day I was reading a book of Mr. Underwood, The Drifted Sands of Party Politics, in which he says that the friends of low tariff in the United States deplored the defeat in Canada of reciprocity in 1911. He himself was leader of tih-e Democratic party in congress at the time and had supported President Taft in that policy. Indeed, the policy of no truck or Irade when things are going one way, and of retaliation when they are going the otherway does not seem to me quite fair. After all, what we shall have to consider is whether a further raising of the artificial barrier at the border line of our country would be in the interests of our people en masse,'whether it would make for greater prosperity, for greater harmony, for larger progress in our own country, whatever may be the effect on other countries. There lies the whole principle, and any other argument seems rather to be camouflaged rhetoric.
I should like to refer to one or two other matters but I am afraid my time is going. However, there is another question which I desire particularly to discuss, and I will come to it immediately. Canada can compete with the world, and is competing with the world, not with the weapons of retaliation, of distrust, of fear, of -economic or other warfare, but with the weapons of sound organization, the energy of our people, easier transportation, better marketing, and credit being given to our citizens. This is done by leadership, by such -leadership as has given to this country the policy of British preference, which I desire
to discuss for a minute or two in connection with the su-bame-ndment which has been moved.
The subamen-dment, I am free to confess, is rather a shrewd motion,. My hon. friends directly opposite have declared themselves to be afraid of the closing of the market which is nearer to us; my hon. friend from Battle River (Mr. Spencer) indicates to them other markets-he does so in this sub-amendment. Hon. gentlemen directly opposite have tried indeed to lead the hon. gentleman in the far corner to a stand against the government; but my hon. friend from Battle River is trying to align them behind himself in his own stand against us. Of course, this subamendment cannot be accepted by the government, and no one knows that better than the mover of the subamen-dment. It is a motion of want of confidence. The Minister of Finance has moved that the house resolve itself inito committee of ways and means; my hon. friend from Battle River says: No; the house will n-ot resolve itself into committee of ways and means but- instead we will have a declaration for British preference. This of course would mean the defeat of the government, and those of us who have confidence in the government cannot vote for that motion. Even those who may not be in sympathy with all the policies of the government, but who prefer t-he government to any alternative or substitute which might offer itself-and that substitute can be offered only by my hon. friends directly opposite-are also unable to vote for such a motion.. But I go further. What is the necessity for attacking this government on the question of the British preference? Is it fair to attack us on that question? Who were the originators of the British preference policy in Canada? They were the great Liberal leaders, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and W. S. Fielding.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who borrowed the idea from Sir Charles Tupper- absolutely. I can quote you Sir Wilfrid Laurier to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will not discuss that
question with my hon. friend; he is entitled to whatever comfort he can derive from it. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and W. S. Fielding initiated that policy. They made it the basis of the fiscal policy of Canada. We who are their political successors are also preserving that policy with loyalty and with care, and we are proud of the fact. I have always defended the policy of British preference; other markets were almost closed to us and it was necessary that we should find outlets for our Canadian goods. These were admitted into England free of duty, and it was only in the
The Budget-Mr. Lapointe

interests of Canada that we should take advantage of this situation, because I repeat that this was not a sentimental device; this action was taken and has been maintained in the interests of this country.
Was it not a good policy? The very first year after it was adopted, in 1898, our exports to Great Britain mounted from $75,000,000 to $100,000,000. That progression has continued; our exports to Great Britain for the twelve months ending January, 1929, amounted to $446,000,000 in round figures, while our imports amounted to only about $193,000,000. In addition, the goods we imported from Great Britain paid a duty of over $35,000,000, while our own exports entered England free.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order; the
hon. gentleman's time has elapsed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in common with every member on this side of the house, I am very glad indeed to see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) back in his place, apparently fully restored to health. He has spoken to us this afternoon very charmingly, as perhaps he can better than many others, but like other charmers his speech is full of sweet nothings. It is hardly a year since we heard the whole story which was given us again to-day by the Minister of Justice, and I have yet to hear of any formal action on the part of this government indicating that it meant to change its tariff policy in any degree by reason of certain resolutions which were repeated by the minister this aftertioon.
The Minister of Justice takes some credit for reductions in the tariff schedule; he says that Canada has led the way in this respect as he claims that Canada has so often led the way and intends to continue to lead the way in international relations. But my hon. friends to my left, who perhaps are as keen as any to observe changes in the tariff, stated last year, the year before and again this year that the changes in the tariff amounted to nothing at all as far as their interests are concerned. Indeed one hon. member declared, after a computation, that the changes made by way of reductions by the Liberal government over a period of six years amounted in all to something less than one per cent.
The Minister of Justice made rather a protectionist speech; he rather subscribed to the policy supported by the party on this side of the house, to which we have adhered for years, that we shall so draw our tariff schedules that they will take care of our own country and protect, so far as they can be fairly protected, those industries both agri-

cultural and mechanical which have a right to exist in this country. However, the minister went one step further and spoiled that protectionist idea; he inferred, although he was careful not to put it in words, that he is disposed to let some economic conference meeting in Geneva settle the tariff question for Canada. First and foremost in that conference, according to the minister, were representatives from the United States. That country now proposes to put up its tariff once more, and if I take any meaning at all from the remarks of the Minister of Justice they were designed perhaps to say nice things, to vaunt his patriotism, but perhaps more than that to make some sort of gesture to the United States.
In 1923 Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, in presenting his budget speech, put on record the determination of the Liberal government to make overtures to the United States looking to reciprocity, and in fact he did communicate to the United States that his government were open to a discussion with regard to a reciprocity treaty. This was after 1911, and if the Democratic party, which unfortunately for itself never has been in power since, could not carry its views throughout the whole country, according to this Liberal government, the Republican government, if it regretted the defeat of the treaty of 1911, has had the opportunity since 1923 of concluding a treaty with this country having the same effect.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why stir up the dead?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not stirring up the
dead; I am just laying it away. The minister works himself up almost into a passion over the idea that this party has in mind an economic war against the United States. If that is so I have not heard of it. I fully subscribe to everything the minister has said as to the right of this country to look after its own affairs and the right of the citizens of the United States to elect representatives who will legislate for the benefit of the citizens of that country. That is their business and not ours. But, Mr. Speaker, the remedy suggested by my hon. friend is that we seek new markets; if we cannot find a market in the United States we should go abroad for new markets. Let me say to the minister that he does not need to go out of this country for markets. Let him and his government take such steps as will conserve the industries of Canada and make them prosperous, self-supporting and beneficial to all the people of this country. Let him and his government take even one step towards helping these industries in such a way that the home market in Canada will be maintained for alt

The Budget-Mr. Geary
their products; let us look to the home market instead of looking far across the seas. That will be much simpler and much better for us and, as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) said on Friday, that is what the government has signally failed to do.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Might I ask my hon.
friend just how large a population it will take to consume our 500,000,000 bushels of wheat?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not too good at arithmetic, so I will let my hon. friend work that out himself. If it were at all relevant I would have pleasure in discussing the question with him.
Now I wish to say a few words with regard to the budget, Mr. Speaker, although there is very little to be said as to the financial proposals contained therein. The budget has been called innocuous, but I would hardly agree with that description. To me the financial proposals are not innocuous; they are harmful in that they do not lay down or propose any constructive action on behalf of the people of this country. To that degree they are not innocuous but positively harmful. Hon. gentlemen opposite have said the same; perhaps they are not cold in their reception of the budget but at least they are lukewarm. My hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) says the budget is a parcel of bare bones, but the government need not worry; he will swallow it. To my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Glen) the budget is a negative budget but he will vote in the affirmative for its adoption. He vociferously regrets that the budget contains no measure of relief to the farmers, but he will vote against the amendment expressing in terms that regret. However, the hon. member has one reason for congratulating the government; there is an omission which pleases him very much: The income tax has not been cut this year. How touching it is, Mr. Speaker, to recall the loyalty and devotion to the government of the hon. gentleman who, just one short year ago, joined with the government in voting for a 10 per cent reduction in the income tax.
Finding no particular gratification in the financial proposals, my hon. friends opposite turn to the surplus and the consequent reduction in the debt. I agree that is a matter for congratulation; it might well give them some feeling of pride, but under the conditions which exist to-day there is no difficulty whatever for any government prepared to maintain a certain level of taxation to produce within reasonable limits almost any surplus required. The only financial calls upon the government to-day are the ordinary expenditures of the country and the usual, stereotyped capital expenditure. The time has passed when war expenditures, railway advances and demobilization costs must be met from the funds of Canada, and no one knows that better than the minister. If I were to make any objection to or any criticism of the surplus I would say it was too large. I am given to understand that that amount is not required to amortize and pay off the national debt of this country. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is apportioning some 860,000,000 towards the reduction of the national debt, but the hon. members for South Wellington (Mit Guthrie) and Toronto East Centre (Mr. Matthews) developed a plan for the consideration of the minister whereby the sum of nineteen or twenty million dollars would be set aside each year for a certain number of years and thus in time dissipate the whole national debt. If that scheme be sound, to my mind the Minister of Finance has no right to proceed on the present unscientific basis, and take some $60,000,000 out of the people of Canada when, by a more scientific method, $20,000,000 would answer the same purpose.
The public accounts for 1928, the last year for which they are (complete-every figure I use will be taken from that volume-show that the annual average surplus of the Conservative government for the six years 1917 to 1922 amounted to
S66,000,000, while the annual average surplus of this government in the succeeding six years, from 1923 to 1928, was only $64,000,000. In spite of the difficulties under which they had to work, and in spite of the strain to which they were subject at that time, the Conservative government had an annual surplus which amounted to $2,000,000 more than the annual surplus of the present government since 1923. There is not much comfort in that for the hon. gentlemen opposite, especially when they consider that during the last six years the government has been in office the full man power of the country has been engaged in the industries of field, forest and mine. They were years of bountiful crops, but the six years which preceded them were, first, years during which the business of this country was carried on under a very heavy strain; years when business and production were at a low ebb, and, second, the equally depressing post-war period, during which the country was using every effort to recover from the effects of the Great war. No comparison is fair which compares the last six years with the six years immediately preceding.
The Budget-Mr. Geary

My hon. friends take much comfort in saying that in the last five years there has been a reduction in the national debt, and that the Conservative party were not able to reduce it but were forced to increase it during the preceding six years. How do reductions or additions in the national debt come about? Leaving borrowings to one side the money to be used by the government comes from, first, the consolidated fund into which go all the ordinary receipts from taxation, and, second, a small account which is called special receipts. Normally this latter account does not amount to much but it has been a very advantageous account for the present government, because they have been able to take
835,000,000 from that account during the last six years, as against 83,000,000 during the preceding six years.
The consolidated fund has to take care of the ordinary expenditures of the country, and it normally can take care also of the ordinary stereotyped capital expenditures of the country exclusive of the special expenditures for railway advances and subsidies, and war and demobilization costs. If there is a surplus in the consolidated fund and it has to be used to pay capital or special expenditures, then there is nothing left to apply on the reduction of the debt. To the extent to which money has to be paid on those accounts in excess of the balance in the consolidated fund there is an increase in the public debt. On the other hand, if there is nothing to be paid out of that balance, then there is correspondingly a decrease in the public debt. Keeping in mind then the fact that the preceding government had a surplus each year which amounted to $2,000,000 more than the present government, why is it the national debt was increased during the Conservative regime and has been decreased during the regime of the present government? We will have to turn to the capital account and special expenditure accounts to find the answer. First, let us take, the capital expenditure account; this is the capital account which covers the ordinary stereotyped capital expenditures of the country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Welland canal is an instance.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As the hon. leader of the
opposition (Mr. Bennett) has said, there are canals like the Welland and Trent, and there are also government railways which come under this heading. The only item at the present time under the heading "railways" is the Hudson Bay railway. Only two or three million dollars per year has been expended during the last few years, but in former years

there were items of $25,000,000 and $30,000,000 and so on, deficits on operation of the Intercolonial railway. During those years we had the Intercolonial under our control, but that deficit has disappeared because of the action of the Conservative government in amalgamating that railway with the National railway system.
Another division of the capital occount covers public works, government buildings in Ottawa, the shipbuilding program of the government in power, and certain things like the St. Lawrence ship canal. Those accounts do not vary to any degree from year to year, except by reason of some abnormal condition. As a rule, they can be paid out of the surplus in consolidated fund without any trouble. During the six years when the Conservative government was in power the expenditures on capital account including government railways and the shipbuilding program amounted to $221,000,000; during the last six years, through no change of policy, nor effort of good management, but only by reason of the necessity for the expenditure having disappeared, the Liberal government has been called upon to pay only $94,000,000.
But there are other special expenditures which have to be considered when we compare the two six-year periods; one expenditure is that of war demobilization, and the other is railway advances and subsidies.
It is not necessary to give any detail regarding the railway advances and subsidies. Everyone knows that these were necessary in the process of taking over the decrepit railways of the country and amalgamating them into one'great system. That was an enterprise which was carried out by the Conservative party, and it has since been amply justified in every particular. Under the six years of Conservative rule the government was called upon to advance some $210,000,000, in subsidies and allowances to railways while the present government has had to pay only $131,000,000 during the last six years. In addition the Conservative government assumed the burden of $284,000,000 nonactive assets representing previous advances to the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk and Canadian Northern Railways.
The third special expenditure account is that of war and demobilization. During the six years of the Conservative regime the government had to expend $1,462,000,000, on this account while the Liberal government during its term of office has had to expend only $8,000,000.
The addition of these capital and special expenditures Shows that the Conservative gov-

The Budget-Mr. Geary
eminent were called upon, to expend $2,177,000,000, whereas the present government has been saddled with only $233,000,000. Is it any wonder that the public debt of the country was of necessity increased during that period? The people were taxed to the limit and no one can say that the Conservative party could have taken any more out of the people during those years. The Conservative party increased the debt by $1,807,000,000 or $370,000,000 less than the amount they were obliged to assume or pay out for abnormal capital expenditure for war expenditures and for subsidies and advances to railways. They were able to do that by good financing; not by taking too much money from the people but iby conserving expenditures and showing a balance in consolidated fund which was more than the balance shown under the present government. Through proper management they were able to make a very much better showing with regard to the national debt than that made by the Liberal government which during the past six years has shown a reduction in the national debt of $125,000,000. One would not object very strenuously to all the glory taken, the boasting, if you like to call it so, of hon. members opposite in regard to this showing; but here is the unfair part of it, and it is to this I wish to direct most of my attention. In order to discredit the preceding government or to reflect credit upon themselves, this government and its members persist in comparing, as though they were on a comparable basis, the six years just ending of government by the Liberals with the six years immediately preceding of government by the Conservatives. Of course anyone in his senses knows that as between these two periods there is no proper basis for comparison. One would have thought hon. gentlemen opposite, realizing this, would at least be fair about the matter, but they have been unfair and they have made misstatements which amount to deception. I do not like to think hon. members would make such statements deliberately, and I can only ascribe their doing so to lack of knowledge of the true state of affairs and lack of attention to the public accounts. More flagrant than anyone else on the opposite side in this unfair comparison have been the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself and one of the members of his government. The Prime Minister has been time and again called to account for it but he still persists in making the same representations in regard to which he was corrected and which he must honestly know are at least that sort of deception that is more dangerous than
the truth-a half truth. It is not long since the Prime Minister had occasion to speak about this same matter and he said that the public debt in 1919 had been increased by hon. gentlemen opposite-that is by this party-to the tune of $382,000,000. That is perfectly true. The impression to be left, apparently willingly by him, was that in the normal course of affairs the debt had been increased by that vast amount by a Conservative government. My leader (Mr. Bennett) corrected him saying:
That was direct payment for railways.
As a matter of fact during that year it was more for demobilization, but my right hon. friend did not know that, because he replied:
Mr. Mackenzie King:	Not at all. It was
made up of the general expenditures of hon. gentlemen opposite including these grants.
That is railway grants. Could anything be more unfair than that? It is as though he ignored a tremendous, special expenditure of millions upon millions of dollars and emphasized a small expenditure made in the ordinary routine out of the consolidated fund and out of the revenues of the country. It is just as though the right hon. gentleman had likened a mouse to an elephant because they were of the same colour; there is no more logic than that in making such a comparison. He went on to say:
In the next year

That is 1920.
-there was not a direct payment for railways and yet in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1920, the public debt of Canada was further increased by over $674,000,000.
And here I object.
That is the way in which the country was being governed while hon. gentlemen opposite were in office in 1919 and 1920.
The implication is that the money was wasted. The. truth is that the money was spent on the most righteous of purposes, largely in carrying on the war in which this country was engaged at the moment, and in amalgamating and giving to the people under public ownership a great national system of railways. That" is the -way the country was being governed, and we are proud of .the fact that it was being governed in that way during those years. Canada will never cease to bless the Conservative government of those years for the fact that they brought into being under public ownership the Canadian National Railways and that they so prosecuted their efforts in regard to the conduct of .the war that with the troops supporting them, they
The Budget-Mr. Geary

brought great glory to Canada. That is the way the country was 'being governed, and we take great pride in the fact.
My right, hon. friend was again interrupted by my leader when he made a statement of the same sort. My leader said:
Due to the war.
My right hon. friend replied:
Due to their methods of financing. . . . We reduced expenditures and imposed some increased taxation for the purpose, mark you, to meet obligations which were left to us by the previous administration. At first about all that we were able to do was to hold the deficit at the point at which it had been the year before. The deficit instead of being $92,000,000 was brought down to $81,000,000 in 1922.
The right hon. gentleman and his cabinet had nothing whatever to do with bringing that down from 192,000,000 to $81,000,000. Mr. Fielding said that it was no part of the present government's work to deal with the spending of money in the fiscal year thpre referred to. The deficit was reduced by only $11,000,000, it is true, but it was reduced because conditions were improved. The present government had no hand in decreasing the deficit; it was none of their business at all. In spite, however, of the corrections of the right hon. gentleman's statement, he persists and his colleagues persist in that unfair and misleading comparison of those years of Liberal rule with the preceding years of Conservative rule.
The right hon. gentleman then went on to say that in 1923 his government began to function by way of imposing more taxation and reducing expenditures. An examination of the books will show that they did nothing in regard to reducing expenditures. There was a falling off of some $13,000,000 or $14,000,000 in expenditures, but this was not due to any change, because the expenditures of the departments, taking them by and large, about balanced with those of the preceding years. There were some millions of dollars less for elections and for pensions and other items which account for the decrease, but none of this was due to any change in policy on the part of the government. They said that the revenue was increased. The revenue was increased to the extent of $4,000,000 by taxes that bore so hardly upon the people that they had to take them off the next year.
They had to retrace their steps and take off many of those nuisance taxes which were not meeting with the approval of the people. The smaller increase in this debt that year was due to the fact that a great deal more money came through customs; some $10,000,000 came 
in from war refunds and there was a much smaller payment necessary for railway advances.
There is only one other speaker to whom I wish to refer and that is the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). He is not in his seat, but I shall not refrain on that account from saying what I desire to say. As reported on page 1029 of Hansard, after making the same invidious comparison, unfair and misleading as he should have known it to be, he made the following statement:
When my hon. friend compared the period of 1918 to 1922 with the period of 1925 to 1929, he made a comparison concerning a different Canada altogether.
With that I quite agree. That has been the burden of my remarks. Why was it a different 'Canada? He goes on to say:
A Canada which had emerged from the gloom which existed during the last five years of Conservative rule and had entered into the sunlight of prosperity under Liberal rule.
Probably that statement is put more unfairly than any of the other statements that have been made. The hon. gentleman was taking part in the war; he was doing his gallant best; he believed he was right; he surely believed the government was right, why at this stage should he take sides against the government which was endeavouring so to hold up our hands over there in France that success would ultimately attend the efforts of the forces. I do not think two years ago he would have said any such thing, but he says he is prepared to subscribe to that, to say the least, disingenuous statement of his leader and for that he must accept full responsibility himself. He is making a statement and a comparison, ignoring the heroic efforts of the people at home to maintain the forces in the field. That is exactly what he is doing.

In addition there was $284,000,000, representing advances to the Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Northern railways which had been carried for a time as a non-active asset, but which was wiped out, quite properly, by the Conservative government of the day and added to the national debt. The balance was extended to the amount of $10,000,000 in one year, and $10,000,0001 in another year, in advances to the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian National Railways were beginning to prosper, but they could not prosper at the beginning. They are prospering now only because the Conservative government in those six years preceding welded the scattered units into one great system and started the national system on its way. My hon. friend will have to admit that he himself opposed it in the session of 1919, and the battle was fought oveT their protesting and beaten bodies, and it was over their bodies that the Conservative party passed to the making of this great national railway. It is now beginning to pay. That is because it was a well-considered and well-advised scheme. It looked to the true interests of the country. no faith, men fearful of results, men without vision. Frank Cochrane, at that time Minister of Railways, and his colleagues in the government, declared that in undertaking this work they were looking to the day when there would be a great waterway from the head of the lakes to tidewater. I think my hon. friend the Minister of Justice referred to the British preference. Let him take what comfort he can for his party from that policy; I do not think he can point to one major development of this country that in any manner, shape or form can be ascribed to the Liberal party. Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford): Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part briefly in this debate, may I as a member from western Canada congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) upon the splendid financial statement which he has brought down for the approval of the house. It has been said that the popularity of budgets is something like the greatness of great men- some men are bom great, some achieve greatness, and others have greatness thrust upon them. The budgets brought down by the hon. Minister of Finance for the last few years have become popular from three points of view. First, they are connected with a party that believes in retrenchment and in financial reform, a party with a financial history of which any Canadian ought to be proud. So this budget grows out of the viewpoint of the Minister of Finance, the viewpoint of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the viewpoint of the Liberal party in a financial sense; consequently it has grown in popularity since its introduction. And secondly, Mr. Speaker, it has become more popular because of the fact that it contains within itself the inherent qualities of popularity and stability. So notwithstanding the speeches we have had, some for and some against the budget, the opinion developed in this house is helping wonderfully in the formation of public opinion in its behalf throughout the Dominion and bringing about a condition of affairs that tends to make the budget appeal more and more to the people of Canada as the days go by. A further and a third reason for the popularity of the budget is that it is framed by the Finance minister with reference to the international situation. No budget not recognizing present-day international developments could really be a strong budget. Therefore this is a budget upon which Canada can courageously stand so far as its relationship is concerned not only with its neighbour across the International boundary but with the other nations of the world.
The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), speaking of the prosperity of Canada, admitted that Providence had showered all sorts of prosperity on this nation [DOT]

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh
but he qualified his statement by saying that the inclination of himself and of his party both in the house and in the country was that Providence and the people of Canada were to a major extent responsible for the prosperity announced in the budget. The hon. gentleman's theology and philosophy do not seem to be very sound. Providence does not cooperate by direct action; Providence cooperates through individuals and through governments to bring about national progress, national development and national prosperity. Providence inspires men to take action to organize a system of government that legislation may be passed for the welfare of the people generally. In other words, governments are the media through which national progress takes place. So Providence in cooperating with the people of Canada to bring about the splendid state of affairs which now obtains goes one better than did the good Tories of Toronto every time the late Sir Wilfnd Laurier visited that great city. They would turn out to hear him, they would listen to him, they would applaud him, but on election day-they would vote against him. Providence with Liberalism in the saddle goes beyond that kind of cooperation. He not only makes it possible for the Liberal part}' to come into power in Canada but when they are in power he cooperates with them in such a way that Canada's financial record is something of which we should all be proud.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in discussing the budget, made reference to the fact that Canada was geographically a very difficult country to govern. We all admit that Canada embraces a large area and is a large country to govern wisely. But we have no colour problem in Canada; we have no major racial problem here. Consequently when we hear hon. gentlemen talking about the difficulty of governing Canada, because of its being a large geographical unit extending from one sea to another, we are inclined to ask whether these hon. gentlemen know Canada from sea to sea, whether they know Canada province by province, whether they know Canada east by west and north by south and whether, knowing it, they understand the sentiments and objectives of the Canadian people. We have a large country to govern, but I believe that if we know our country as we ought and understand our problems as we should we can go forward and make history.
The hon. gentleman also referred to the national policy; he spoke of the notable things it had done for Canada. It was, according to him, a wonderful fiscal policy. But he

did not tell us why in 1896 Canada was stagnant commercially, why Canada was at a standstill industrially, why Canada's imperial and world trade had become very diminutive in quantity. And the point is just this: that although the Conservatives introduced the national policy it took the Liberal party to understand the machine and to operate it in such a way, by adjustment from year to year and from decade to decade, as to promote the development of Canada and to bring about the prosperity and progress which we have to-day in this Dominion. The hon. member referred further to the many things the Conservative party had done from the standpoint of confederation. One would imagine, to hear him talk, that the Conservative party was really responsible for that great movement in Canada

the confederation or union, of all the British North American provinces on the shoulder of this continent and their consolidation from coast to coast, with the proud history which that union has written from that day to this. What are the facts? If we turn to history we shall find it indicated that the Conservative party was not the cause of that great movement-not at all. We know that one cause was the imperative necessity of wiping out the protective tariffs between the different provinces then existing. The protective tariffs of that day were detrimental to the development of trade and also to interprovincial cohesion; their removal became necessary and that was one of the causes of confederation in 1867. Another was the political deadlock which had come about. And still another was this: The people of the provinces were living in dread of the states to the south and consequently they did not feel themselves strong enough in a military . way to combat the people across the boundary line. There we have the three and only causes of confederation, one political, one fiscal and one military. And when the movement took place Liberals and Conservatives combined, hand in hand, to bring about that great union under which Canada has prospered and which we hope will continue to grow stronger and stronger as the years come and go.
When we touch upon the question of confederation. w'hen hon. gentlemen opposite speak of the extraordinary things done by the Conservative party, we ought to bring into the perspective some of the things which the Conservative party have not done. For instance, they did not stand by the Liberal party in fighting for the right to negotiate our own commercial treaties, which right was granted in the year 1907. They did not stand

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh
by the Liberal party in its action for the control of our immigration laws granted us in 1904 and for the bringing into existence of our navigation laws in 1870. They did not stand behind us in 1882 for the veto so far as the nomination of the Governor General is concerned; nor did they support the Liberal party in respect to its policy of securing Canadian representation on the privy council in 1897. And so far as the Ballot Act of 1874 is concerned, a great reform, the Liberal party had to put that act through by itself; and upon the secret ballot, to a large extent, has been built the political liberty and the financial and industrial welfare of this Dominion.
I noticed that the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary), in his speech this afternoon used the term protection, and I was glad to hear him use that term; because sometimes when our hon. friends meet in national convention they seem to run away from it. They appear to be afraid of the expression. The last time-as a matter of fact I believe it was the first time in their history-they had a national convention, when they met in Winnipeg, they considered a resolution on the tariff. A copy of that resolution I have in my hand and that term protection does not appear in it. The resolution was moved by Mr. Haggerman, of Unity, Saskatchewan, a few miles south of the riding I have the honour to represent in this house, and it was spoken to by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). The gentleman who moved the resolution came from one of the grain growing areas of western Canada and the idea was to have this resolution drafted in such a way that it would appeal to that section of the country and the rest of western Canada and thus secure the votes of the farmers and others on election day. Consequently the word protection is not used. In the first paragraph we are told about the wonderful growth, progress and prosperity of Canada under the historic fiscal policy, but the descriptive title of that policy is omitted. The reason for this we leave our hon. friends to explain. In the next paragraph we are told how adherence to this policy has brought about a gratifying development in Canada. We have heard quite a lot of discussion with regard to our national debt. I desire to touch that question briefly, and the thought comes to me that in discussing the national debt we should compare the records of both great political parties from confederation. This afternoon the hon. member for South Toronto said it was not fair to compare the reductions made in the national debt during the last few years, because the Conservatives were in power during the war and we should be as fair as possible and give them all the credit to which they are entitled. I want to do that, but I think it fair to compare the records of the two great parties on this matter from 1867 to 1929. When parties are in power they must accept responsibility; if a war comes along or upheavals of different kinds take place of course the party in power must accept the responsibility.
On March 31, 1928, our national debt was 12,296,850,232.92, and we are told that the estimated debt as of March 31, 1921, is $2,227,068,000. This year the reduction is approximately $69,000,000, and during the last six years we have paid off $226,708,000, or an average per year of $37,700,000. Previous to that the Liberal government made reductions in the national debt in 1900, 1903, 1904 and 1907; these reductions totalled $14,216,035, and if we add that amount to the reduction of $226,000,000 during the last six years we have a total reduction of $240,924,035. If that sum is divided by the twenty-eight years the Liberals have been in power we get exactly the amount

the Liberals as a .party have reduced our national debt. I think that is an eminently fair way of getting at the question in order to find out just what the Liberals and Conservatives have each done in the way of financially redeeming Canada; that is what each party has done by a policy of financial retrenchment and reform towards the solution of all the financial problems concerning Canada. We find that the Liberals have made an average annual reduction in the national debt of $8,571,428 for every year they have been in office. Now let us consider what the Conservatives have done. They were in power in Canada during thirty-four years; in 1871 they reduced the debt by $503,225; in 1882 by $1,734,129, in 1912 by $122,591 and in 1913 by $25,617,836. In other words, during their thirty-four years in office they reduced the national debt by about $27,000,000, which works out at the rate of about four-fifths of a million per year, or $822,875, to be exact.
There you have the record of the Liberals as compared with that of the Conservatives. The Liberals have faced the question of the national debt as a great responsibility; they have gone to work and reduced it, as any party should. From year to year the record of the Liberal party in connection with reductions in the national debt has been a splendid one, and it appears that year by year that record is getting better, because the cut of .practically $70,000,000 this year is the largest reduction ever made. In thirty-four years the Conservative party made only four attempts to out down the national debt, yet since the budget has been brought down hon. gentlemen opposite have been telling us what we should do to reduce the debt. We have been told that we should abandon the policy that we have followed since 1922 and1 adopt a fixed method of paying off the debt over a term of years, and we have been told many times that the present leadership of the party is not as successful as it should be with regard to this great .problem. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and his cabinet and Liberals generally are very well satisfied with what has been done by the .party as a whole during the last nine years. We are told .that we are not going fast enough and that we should inaugurate a sinking fund scheme in order to pay off the debt in forty or fifty yearn. If we continue the progress we have maintained since 1925 the national debt of Canada will be paid off in twenty-four years. Since 1925 we have reduced the debt by an average of $47,750,000 yearly, and if we continue at that rate for the next twenty-four years we will wipe out our national debt.

It seems to me that this is a splendid record, but I have 'before me an article which appeared in Willison's Monthly, written by a Doctor H. P. Spaulding, in which he takes the opposite stand and says we are paying off our debt too quickly. He states that the Liberal party is using a sort of whirlwind method, that we are paying off sums of money from year to year which are too large, and that we should change our system and for the next five years pay $10,900,000 off the debt yearly. That would give us a reduction of $50,000,000,and we are told that at the end of the five-year period we should add $1,000,000 to that amount for the following thirty-five years, which would result in the national debt being wiped off in twenty-four years. In other words', Doctor Spaulding thinks we are going too fast, but to me that seems a very good proof that our policy with regard to this great question is sound. I believe that in times of peace we should face our national debt and reduce it as much as possible; we are responsible for the creation of that debt, and we Should not lea/ve it to be paid by posterity. When times are good we should reduce the debt as much as possible. It is not like building a hall for which posterity must pay, when they may have the use of rhe hall; this is an obligation which we should take seriously and solve in a way that will be to the greatest benefit to Canada as a nation.
So, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the national debt I would say we are going at it in the right way: I think we should continue just as we a.re doing at present until 1933 and 1934, when practically a billion dolare of our war debt will come due. That amount is all owed in Canada; when that comes due we should face that problem in all its aspects, and if we think we should do something different then let us evolve another policy and follow it through. However, with respect to our present method, I would say it is good, and I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and the government on the wonderful financial record of this party during the last eight or nine years. I believe there is not a citizen of Canada who wants to be fair who would not say that the financial record of this government is bright and splendid and an honour to Canada.

When we come to solve the question of our fiscal problems with the United States we should not forget that we have a party possessing objectives as high and noble and as patriotic as any party could have. When we face that question I say, we are certainly going to solve it in a way which will be beneficial to our population as a whole.
Some people are wondering whether we shall be able to make the right kind of a bargain fiscally with the United States. Personally, I am not a bit afraid. I will stake a cabinet of Canadians against any cabinet in the world when it comes to bartering or organizing a fiscal policy which will be of lasting benefit to the country. Neither is there any danger of absorption by the United States nor by any other nation through the investments which have been made in this country. This is our present standing. Government securities in Canada total $4,200,000,000 and less than one-third of that total, or $1,300,000,000, is controlled outside of Canada. Surely we do not need to be afraid of economic control in regard to government securities. Railway securities total $3,500,000,000 and of that $1,400,000,000 is controlled outside of Canada. Mining stocks total $650,000,000 and one-half of that is controlled outside of Canada. Industrial securities total $4,050,000,000 and $1,300,000,000 of that is controlled outside of Canada. Trading establishment securities total $2,000,000,000, 90 per cent of which is controlled in Canada. Other public utilities total $3,100,000,000 and only one-third is controlled outside of Canada. In other words, out of a total of $16,000,000,000 of securities, only about $5,500,000,000 or one-third is controlled outside of Canada. So, financially speaking, I would say that we are on solid ground and, fiscally speaking, if our party and our leaders follow the reputation and the history of tbs Liberal party of the past, there will be no doubt about the future of Canada irrespective of what nation says: We will trade with you, or we will not trade with you.
In closing, I believe that while financial retrenchment is one principle of the Liberal

party and fiscal reform another, there is still a further principle of great importance and Canada ought to be admired for adhering to it. That other principle which belongs to historic Liberalism is the principal of peace and the peace treaty that the Prime Minister of Canada signed last year in August in Paris is a proof that Canada is determined to play her part not only nationally but in an imperial and a world way in connection with international affairs,-that in a way I am sure will be gratifying to all Canadians. The Liberal party stands on the foundation principle of peace. It stands for internal peace, peace between one province and another, peace between the east and the west; peace, progress and development between Canada and the rest of the empire and peace with other nations. The idea is simply banishing wiar as an instrument of national policy and putting in its place the principle of peace. The sooner we take the lead in that-and we are doing so- the better for Canada. With regard to the question of peace not only within Canada but with other nations of the world we know that fiscally the Liberal party is doing what it can to work out a policy that will be of benefit to the whole Dominion.
Finally, in regard to Canada's relationship with the motherland, Sir James Owen, after visiting Canada in 1927, had this to say:
The Canadians are developing along their own lines. One hears sometimes that they are being Americanized. There are no obvious signs of that. The Canadian does not speak like an American, nor does he think as an American. His outlook on life is less flamboyant than that of his neighbours across the border. There is in the Canadian a sobriety, a restraint, such as one would expect of a people who derive so largely from Scottish ancestry.
Then again Sir James says:
Whether Canada will indefinitely remain a member of the British Empire is for the Canadians to say.
To that we will answer in the affirmative. He continues:
I think the chances are that, having achieved their independence for all practical purposes, being linked to Great Britain and the empire by bonds intangible and spiritual, rather than material, the connection will persist, and may well become stronger with the passage of time, an,d. the inevitable development of _ a common empire policy. But, whatever the future may have in store for us all, I am persuaded that Canadians will not surrender their independence, their nationhood, to become a mere appendix to the United States.

I well remember, Mr. Speaker, the year 1904, when representatives of the Liberal government came to the city of Halifax; these included Right Hon. W. S. Fielding and the then Halifax representative, Mr. William Roche, who later was appointed to the Senate.
I attended the meeting, and these two gentlemen asked the people of Halifax and the people of Nova Scotia to give them a mandate to build the Transcontinental railway, promising .that if this mandate were given it would mean a tremendous benefit to the port of Halifax. That mandate was given; the people of Halifax and of Nova Scotia believed in the pledged words of those prominent politicians and sent a solid representation from Nova Scotia, fully believing that if they did so it would mean a tremendous benefit to the port of Halifax and to Nova Scotia generally. To-dlay, sir, I ask that those promises and those pledges be fulfilled, just as I have asked that the promises and pledges made by public, men at the time of confederation should be kept. We are not here from the naaritimes, as has been pointed out before, as supplicants or mendicants; we only ask for these things because we are partners in this great business, this great confederation known as the Dominion of Canada. We came into confederation believing that justice would be done to the maritime provinces, and we are demanding that the pledges and promises which were given be fulfilled. I put this matter up directly to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), and ask that he bend every energy, use every influence at his command and obtain the support of his colleagues on that side of the house toward preventing the carrying out of the requests contained in the resolutions of the Montreal grain exchange and the Montreal board of trade. With his tremendous influence I know he can prevent the granting of these selfish and sectional requests.
I do not wish my remarks to be interpreted as being anti-American. I give credit to the great country to the south of us for the excellent management of their affairs, but I ask the government of this country to exercise the same care in administering |the affaire of Canada. Canada has a great future;*it is a country with wonderful possibilities and splendid 'resources of the farm, forest, sea

I have listened with a great deal of interest to most of the speeches, and while I cannot refer to all of them, I would like to discuss some of the remarks which were made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Quinn).
In concluding his remarks the hon. member referred to speeches delivered by Mr. Fielding and the late Hon. Mr. Roche with regard to the Transcontinental railway. Although the hon. member did not intend to do it, he paid a compliment to the Liberal party when he spoke of the building and the completion of that road. If Mr. Fielding's ideas and the ideas of the Liberal party had been carried out, more grain would be flowing over the Transcontinental to the port of Halifax than is the case at the present time. When the Liberal party was defeated in 1911, and when our Conservative friends came into power, instead of trying to build up the port of Halifax through the construction of that road, they started in to cut the grades down and put in wooden bridges instead of the iron bridges which had been contemplated by the Liberal party and the Transcontinental commissioners. Therefore, the Conservative party and not the Liberal party is to blame for the fact that more traffic is not going through the port of Halifax to-day.

But there are two Duncan reports. One is known as the federal Duncan report, and the other is known as the provincial Duncan report, and I am going to make a comparison to show how the Conservative government in Nova Scotia carried out the provincial Duncan report, and how the Liberal government at Ottawa carried out the federal Duncan report.
The provincial Duncan commission was appointed before the federal commission, and although the former commission long since reported to the premier of Nova Scotia, Mr. Rhodes, not one thing has been done about it. There has been no attempt made by the provincial government to carry out that Duncan report, and let me say in answer to my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) that most of that Duncan report referred to conditions in the mining area in Cape Breton. If any government has the responsibility of looking after the conditions of the workingmen in the province of Nova Scotia, it is the government of that province, and not the federal government.
Now what did the federal government do with regard to the federal Duncan report? We reduced the freight rates in the province of Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces some 20 per cent, giving relief to the people of the maritime provinces to the amount of about $3,000,000 a year. The Canadian National railways gave over a very large amount to the province of Nova Scotia for provincial and municipal taxes, and the Con-

servative government in power at Halifax, instead of passing part of that along to the municipalities, put it all in their own treasury. This parliament also passed legislation with respect to coking plants, to ensure that coal from the mining areas in Cape Breton, and from Stellarton and Springhill, should be used in the manufacture of coke. Then, sir, we gave a special grant of $200,000 to move coal during the winter months from Nova Scotia to Montreal and points further west. We also appointed harbour commissions for the ports of Halifax and St. John; and while I cannot discuss those harbour commissions, there is no doubt that money has been spent freely in the maritime provinces because of those appointments. Then $700,000 was voted for the erection of that great cold storage plant at Halifax.
The Duncan report recommended that certain districts in Nova Scotia should be given railway communication. I want to thank the government and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), the minister from Nova Scotia (Mr. Ralston) and the Canadian National Railways management for arranging that this session the Guysborough railway bill should again come before parliament. I hope and trust in the interests of that part of Nova Scotia that the House of Commons and the Senate will pass the bill so that the railway may be built in the very near future. In addition to providing money for the Guysborough railway this Liberal government- although the riding is represented by a Conservative-is setting aside $375,000 for the Inverness railway.

The Duncan report recommended that till such time as a conference had been held and the matter of subsidies investigated, a lump sum payment should be made to each of the three maritime provinces, and in the case of Nova Scotia they named an annual payment of $875,000. fathom, this government were so generous that they carried out the Duncan report in this respect 150 per cent and gave the provincial government $875,000, plus $437,500. I do not agree with this.

One hon. gentleman on the other side of the house spoke of the conflicting interests in the various sections of this great country. Two years ago I voted with the government to increase the duty on slack coal to 50 cents. This was all right; but certainly as a Liberal and a low-tariff man I would not agree to a further increase in this duty. If it were raised, say, from 50 cents to a dollar a ton, it would only mean that the consumers in this country would have to pay the extra price.
But 'there is a remedy, sir. I said, in answer to my hon. friend, that conditions in the mining area were better this year than they have been for a long time. The men are getting more days' work now than they have been in past years. But certain tilings

Then let us consider the dairy industry, which has been so greatly affected by New Zealand butter coming into Canada practically free of duty. The resolution is as follows:
Whereas, in consequence of the persistent tendency to carry on dairying on too slender a margin of profit, or even at a loss, has resulted in a corresponding failure to cope with the ever growing demand of the home market, not to mention export trade for milk, cream, butter, cheese and ice cream supplied; and
Whereas the consequent shortage of the home made creamery pasteurized butter has resulted in opening the door widely to the importation of this necessary product from, other parts of the empire under treaty privilege, thus enabling New Zealand butter, for instance, to be sold in Canada at prices with which Canadian dairymen cannot compete; and
Whereas the farmer who produces milk for human consumption is also so hemmed in by government regulations of health and standardization that his expenses have increased without any appreciable increase in his income; and
Whereas the dairy industry is now in such a state as to require an effective stimulant and guarantee of stability to bring about the necessary improvements and development to ensure progress and prosperity;
Therefore be it resolved that we members of the Nova Scotia Farmers' Association in annual convention assembled, do ask the federal government at once to increase the tariff on butter from the existing four cents to, say ten cents per pound, or to such a rate that after allowing the preference of three cents per pound, will give the butter industry sufficient protection to enable its paying the producers a rate that will be adequate to yield a reasonable profit on their investment of money and labour.
